title: How Meristems Keep a Plant Growing

scenes.visual: Silent title card: How Meristems Keep a Plant Growing. Show an oak with growing tips and a widening trunk.

scenes.tts: A three hundred year old oak still makes new shoots and wood. It keeps regions of dividing cells, called meristems, for as long as it lives. These supply new cells and organs. That is how many plants keep building their bodies for years. Apical meristems at root and shoot tips add length. Lateral meristems add girth.
scenes.visual: Open on an old oak, with new shoots and a fresh wood ring highlighted. Zoom into dividing cells labelled meristems. Locate apical meristems at root and shoot tips and lateral meristems around the woody stem. Show length and girth arrows; title: How Meristems Keep a Plant Growing.

scenes.tts: Follow a root tip. Under its protective cap, small cells divide in the zone of division. In the zone of elongation, cells stop dividing and lengthen as water fills their vacuoles. In the zone of maturation, they become their final types, and root hairs appear.
scenes.visual: Reuse the root cell file and protective cap. Animate division, vacuole expansion and maturation in sequence, with labelled zones and root hairs on the epidermis. Keep the meristem visible as the source of new cells.

scenes.tts: Division supplies cells. Elongation sets their length. At steady state, with every cell file alike, root growth rate equals new cells per file per hour times final cell length. Take illustrative numbers. One cell per hour times three hundred micrometres gives three hundred micrometres per hour. These numbers are not from a measured species.
scenes.caption: Division supplies cells. Elongation sets their length. At steady state, with every cell file alike, root growth rate equals new cells per file per hour times final cell length. Take illustrative numbers. 1 cell per hour times 300 µm gives 300 µm per hour. These numbers are not from a measured species.
scenes.visual: Show one root cell file and the growth equation, with production and final length colour matched to the zones. Display the steady-state and alike-files assumptions. Work only 1 cell per hour × 300 µm = 300 µm per hour. Label the example illustrative, not a measured species; remove the three-scenario bar chart.

scenes.tts: Now look at the oak trunk. Its vascular cambium adds secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward. Secondary xylem is wood. A different meristem, the cork cambium, makes cork outward and living phelloderm inward. Together with the cork cambium, these form the periderm, replacing the epidermis. Bark is everything outside the vascular cambium. It includes living phloem.

Bracket secondary phloem plus periderm as bark, outside the vascular cambium. Do not show the old normal-growth arithmetic.

scenes.tts: These new cells build tissues. Xylem and phloem are complex tissues, each made of several cell types. They connect plant organs. Xylem carries water. Phloem carries sugars and amino acids. Together they belong to the vascular tissue system.

scenes.visual: Show roots, stem and leaves connected by vascular tissue. Label water transport in xylem and sugars and amino acids in phloem. Inset multiple cell types within each tissue and label the shared vascular tissue system. Replace the blocked-elongation animation.

scenes.tts: In a leaf, veins carry both tissues. Chloroplasts in the mesophyll capture light. Air spaces connect to stomata, pores opened and closed by guard cells. An open stoma lets carbon dioxide in and water vapour out. The leaf gains carbon at a cost in water.

Finish on the leaf connected to the growing plant, retaining the carbon gain and water loss arrows.
